record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: Can communication in federated learning be reduced substantially further, and what are the practical optimal trade-offs between communication cost and model accuracy once the optimization algorithm is taken into account rather than abstracted away?

evidence.quote: However, it remains unclear if communication cost can be further reduced, and whether any of these methods or their combinations can come close to providing optimal trade-offs between communication and accuracy in federated learning. ... It remains an open direction to leverage such statistical approaches to inform practical training methods.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a global model with parameters $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across $N$ clients, where client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ and a local loss $F_i(w) = \mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(w;z)]$. The goal is to (approximately) minimize the global objective $F(w) = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i F_i(w)$ for given weights $p_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i p_i = 1$, by an iterative protocol consisting of $T$ rounds in which, on each round, a subset of clients receive the current model from the server, perform local computation, and transmit a message back; the total number of bits sent on the uplink (and downlink) channels is the communication cost $C$, and the accuracy of the resulting model $\hat w$ is measured by the optimization error $F(\hat w) - \min_w F(w)$ or by the test accuracy on held-out data.

Existing communication-reduction techniques include (i) gradient/model quantization, (ii) sparsification (top-$k$ or random-$k$), (iii) low-rank or sketched updates, (iv) reducing the number of communication rounds via multiple local SGD steps (e.g., FedAvg), and combinations thereof. Restricting attention to algorithms that solve federated optimization problems of the above form under standard assumptions (e.g., $L$-smooth, possibly non-convex local losses, bounded heterogeneity, stochastic gradient access at each client):

(a) Determine whether the total communication cost $C$ required to achieve a target optimization (or generalization) accuracy $\varepsilon$ can be reduced substantially below what is achieved by current methods such as quantized/sparsified FedAvg and its variants.

(b) Characterize the optimal trade-off curve between communication cost $C$ and achievable accuracy $\varepsilon$ for federated optimization, taking the underlying optimization algorithm (its convergence rate, local computation, and client sampling) as an integral part of the problem rather than abstracting it away as in pure information-theoretic distributed estimation lower bounds. In particular, exhibit matching algorithmic upper bounds and lower bounds on $C$ as a function of $\varepsilon$, $d$, $N$, the number of participating clients per round, and the heterogeneity of $\{F_i\}$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broadly stated open research direction in federated learning. Substantial progress has been made on individual compression methods (quantization, sparsification, error feedback, local SGD analysis) and on distributed estimation lower bounds, but a tight characterization of the practical optimal communication–accuracy trade-off that incorporates the optimization algorithm remains an active and unresolved area as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning (survey)
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies the question of optimal communication-accuracy trade-offs in federated learning as an open direction.
status_evidence.claim: The trade-off question is posed as open in the federated learning literature.

status_evidence.title: A Field Guide to Federated Optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys recent algorithms for communication-efficient federated optimization and notes that tight characterizations of trade-offs remain open.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent surveys still treat the optimal communication-accuracy trade-off in federated optimization as not fully resolved.
